title: Kinetic Friction
short: A sliding object feels friction f_k = μ_k N against its sliding.
trouble: Students use mg instead of the normal force when the normal force isn't mg.

blocks.html: When one surface slides over another, friction acts against the sliding. For many pairs of dry surfaces, its size follows a simple rule that depends on the The Normal Force and Apparent Weight.

Kinetic friction: $f_k = \mu_k F_N$, directed opposite to the sliding. The coefficient $\mu_k$ (no units) depends on the two surfaces; typical values run from about $0.03$ (oiled steel on steel) to about $0.7$ (rubber on dry concrete).

Surfaces touch only at tiny bumps. Pressing them together harder flattens the bumps into more contact, and the extra contact resists sliding in proportion. So friction grows with how hard the surfaces press, which is the normal force, not the weight. For a box on level ground those are equal; on a ramp, with an extra push or with a slanted pull, they are not.

opts.task: The cart coasts with no push. Change μ_k and the mass: the slowing depends on μ_k, not on the mass.

blocks.cap: A sliding box slows at a = μ_k g, whatever its mass.

blocks.title: Friction on a level floor
blocks.q: A $25\ \text{kg}$ box slides on a floor with $\mu_k = 0.3$. Find the friction force.

blocks.title: How far it slides
blocks.q: A box sliding at $6\ \text{m/s}$ on a floor with $\mu_k = 0.25$ coasts to a stop. How far does it go?
steps: Friction is the net force: $a = \dfrac{\mu_k mg}{m} = \mu_k g = 2.45\ \text{m/s}^2$ (slowing).

blocks.title: A push from above
blocks.q: You press down on a sliding $25\ \text{kg}$ box with $50\ \text{N}$ ($\mu_k = 0.3$). Find the friction.

blocks.html: Using $mg$ instead of the normal force when they differ. Check: find $F_N$ from the vertical (or perpendicular) forces first, every time; then multiply by $\mu_k$.
